title: Comparing Arctic Macrobenthos Across a Decade (WCMB Talk)
text:
Macrobenthic life in the deep central Arctic Ocean is understudied despite its importance in biogeochemical cycling of carbon and nutrients. Here we focus on the Eurasian Basin that encompasses the Nansen and Amundsen Basins separated by the Gakkel Ridge. We compare macrofauna from a total of 24 box corer samples across 17 stations (3400 – 4400 m depth) in both basins sampled with RV Polarstern in 2012 and 2023. These two years differed notably in the presence and absence of the fast-sinking sea-ice algae Melosira arctica, which was present in 2012 but not in 2023, probably due to unusual sea-ice drift patterns in 2023 that resulted in a shift of the origin of the sea ice, as well as increased open water productivity in 2012.
We identified 63 taxa and as is typical, major taxonomic groups included Polychaeta followed by Bivalvia and specifically in 2023, the brooding crustaceans Isopoda, Amphipoda, Tanaidacea in the Amundsen Basin. Macrofauna density and biomass did not differ significantly between basins within one year indicating no or weak dispersal limitation by the Gakkel Ridge, consistent with previous studies. However, the population of several species sampled in 2012 consisted mostly of adults, whereas in 2023 they were made up mostly by juveniles, indicating a different status of the ecosystem despite the same time of sampling. In line with this, macrobenthic biomass was significantly lower in 2023, which is consistent with lower bacterial abundances and lower food quality, indicated by the proportion of chlorophyll a to total chloroplastic pigments. This difference was especially pronounced in the Amundsen Basin, where a concurrent decrease in macrofauna density was observed. Interestingly, Hill diversity indices were higher in 2023 compared to 2012, mostly driven by the presence of many rare species detected in 2023.
Our results suggest differences in cryo-pelagic-benthic coupling between the years with impacts on benthic life. However, macrofauna diversity, density and biomass varied strongly among stations, reflecting deep-sea patchiness and the need for increased sampling efforts. Regular sampling across seasons is needed to understand potential multiyear changes as the benthos might respond slower in comparison to surface water communities.

title: Vision
text:
ALONGate is an endorsed „UN decade action“ in cooperation with DOOS and Challenger 150.


The boundary region between Iceland, Norway, and Greenland acts as a corridor for specialized fauna to extreme environmental conditions moving through the North Atlantic Gateway to the Arctic Ocean. While a huge amount of biodiversity data is available for this area, the accumulation of data in more frequently sampled regions reveals sampling gaps, especially in deep and remote regions. The ALONGate project studies biodiversity across temporal and spatial gradients and connects data from previously established projects around Iceland (BIOICE: Benthic Invertebrates of Icelandic waters 1992 – 2004 and IceAGE: Icelandic marine Animals: Genetics and Ecology since 2011).

title: Vision
text:
Vision
Since 2023, annual Epibenthic Sledge (EBS) sampling in the HAUSGARTEN long-term ecological observatory established by the Alfred-Wegener-Institute contributes to a fundamental understanding of local warm and cold-water species distributions. Additionally, samples collected on a latitudinal Nord-South transect from Germany to the Fram Strait fill knowledge gaps for future observations of faunal community shifts towards northern waters.
In-situ sampling of latitudinal and longitudinal deep-sea transects throughout the Gateway area is complemented with the deployment of long-term Benthic Lander Observatory Systems (BLOS) at critical intersecting nodes of the North-South and East-West transects, with a special focus on collecting image data of Vulnerable Marine Ecosystems (VMEs) like hydrothermal vents or cold-water coral (CWC) reefs across seasonal changes.
Based on the compiled dataset of abiotic (bathymetric assessments, benthic oxygen uptake measurements, sediment samples) and biotic parameters (macrofauna samples, image data), a comprehensive comparison of macro- and megafauna community will contribute to a better understanding of benthic biodiversity and its driving parameters.

Further introduction

title: Cumaceans in the Deep Arctic Ocean
text:
Our team focused on Cumaceans (also called “comma shrimp”), which are small crustaceans that live on and in the seafloor. Over the past 10 years, using gears like box corers and epibenthic sleds, we sampled deep-sea cumaceans living below 500 m depth at the Hausgarten LTER. Nearly 2200 individual specimens were examined for this study and we found:

Cumacean diversity peaks between 1,200 and 1,500 meters deep
Some species live much deeper than previously known, such as Leucon acutirostris diving deeper for astonishing 3511 meters!
We didn’t find any species that only live below 2,000 meters. Instead, most of these species can thrive across a massive range of depths and are widespread across the Arctic.




Hausgarten LTER is located at Fram Strait between Svalbard and Greenland. It is strongly effected by the local current system: West Spitzbergen Current (WSC), East Greenland Current (EGC), and Return Atlantic Current (RAC).

title: Cumaceans in the Deep Arctic Ocean
section: The First Identification Key for Arctic Cumaceans
text:
The First Identification Key for Arctic Cumaceans
We’ve put together a comprehensive catalogue featuring simplified traditional and digital identification keys for 64 species of deep-sea Cumacea. Based on our models, this list is likely a complete representation of cumacean species in the Arctic deep sea. Because the Central Arctic Ocean has a low uniqueness of taxa, these identification keys can be reliably applied to the entire deep Arctic Ocean.
We also found some surprising physical traits that challenge how we previously classified certain species (especially in the families Diastylidae and Leuconidae), reminding us that the deep sea always has more to teach us.

title: A Long-term Observatory on the Seafloor
text:
BLOS, stands for Benthic Lander Observatory System, is a customized system designed for data collection on the seafloor for a long period of time. Currently, three of such systems have been successfully deployed around Iceland during the MSM145 expedition in 2026.

title: A Long-term Observatory on the Seafloor
text:
Deployment and Recovery
Is the Wifi module originally from us or the Ifremer has used it previously? If it’s from us we need to sell this novelty.
Our BLOS are specifically designed for deployment and recovering using GEOMAR’s ROV Phoca, so that the entire system can be loaded onto the ROV’s porch at one go and brought to the desired spot on the seafloor. Our engineers has came up with a creative solution for setting up the systems: a deep-sea Wi-Fi.
The ROV and the BLOS each hold a Wi-Fi module that allows real-time data transmission from BLOS computer to the ROV. Once the ROV reached the deployment site, the positioning, lighting and camera configuration will be carried out by controlling the BLOS directly from the mission control onboard the vessel. When all settings are done, the Wi-Fi module from the BLOS will be removed from ROV container, detaching the two systems completely.

title: New and Old Isopods
text:
A new isopod species was discovered at the Nidhogg chimney (3016 m) in the Jøtul vent field and the deep-sea Amundsen Basin (4156 m) in the Artic Ocean. Based on the morphological and molecular evidence, a new genus will be erected including the previously described Jaera tyleri Malyutina & Brandt, 2014. Both species from the newly erected genus share a set of traits, that significantly differ from the rest of the typically shallow-water Jaera species. Two of such characters stood out: they were both sampled at abyssal depth, and presumably both feed on bacteria. While J. tyleri was collected on whale bones and grazing on the bacterial community on the bones, the new species were found at an active hydrothermal vent site and presumably feeds on the chemosynthetic bacteria.



CLSM scans of the new isopod species in dorsal and ventral views (Kohlenbach et al., under review)


The necessity of a taxonomic revision of Jaera Leach, 1814 has already been recognized, as well as the enclosing family Janiridae G.O. Sars, 1897, which is proven to be polyphyletic. This study contributes the first step in resolving the systematics of these groups and our understanding to the ecology of isopods inhabiting chemosynthetic environments.



Stations of the sampling campaign, red points indicates the locations where the new species was found (Kohlenbach et al., under review)

title: New and Old Isopods
text:
Disconectes coxalis Kussakin, 1983
Disconectes coxalis was officially described by Kussakin in 1983, but the type materials was lost later. Adding to the only four individuals collected from Canadian Basins from 3100 to 3400 m depth, approx. 70 specimens of this species were collected at the Eurasian part of the Arctic Ocean during the ArcWatch-1 expedition onboard RV Polarstern, exactly 40 years after the species was described. The newly collected specimens will be used for the re-description along with molecular data.
Although being sampled in the central Arctic Ocean, this species has not been found elsewhere, particularly at the Hausgarten LTER in the Fram Strait, which represents the only deep channel connecting Arctic Ocean with other Ocean sectors. Based on this, D. coxalis are suggested to be endemic in the Arctic.
